heading: A Buddhist kingdom on the roof of the trade routes
body: Ladakh's history is shaped, above almost everything else, by its position: a high, arid crossroads between Tibet, Central Asia and the Indian plains. By the first millennium CE it had become a corridor for merchants and Buddhist monks moving between the Silk Route oasis cities of Yarkand, Kashgar and Khotan and the monastic centres of Tibet and Kashmir, with caravans carrying pashmina wool, salt, turquoise and textiles across its high passes. From around the 9th century, Ladakh developed as a distinct Himalayan kingdom with deep cultural and religious ties to Tibet, and it was ruled for nearly four centuries — from 1460 to 1842 — by the Namgyal dynasty, based at Leh, under whom Tibetan Buddhism became the region's defining religious and cultural tradition, expressed in the great monasteries (gompas) still standing across the region today.

That independent kingdom came to an end in the 1830s. A Dogra army under General Zorawar Singh, acting for Raja Gulab Singh of Jammu, invaded Ladakh between 1834 and 1840, and after further campaigns Gulab Singh formally annexed the kingdom in the early 1840s. The Namgyal royal line was not abolished outright but reduced to a small landholding (jagir) at Stok, near Leh, a diminished status the family held all the way through to Indian independence in 1947. Ladakh was then absorbed into the Dogra princely state of Jammu and Kashmir and, after 1947, into the Indian state of the same name, governed as a peripheral region of a state whose politics were centred on the Kashmir Valley.

That changed in 2019: when Parliament's Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act split the former state, Ladakh was separated out as its own union territory, administered directly from Delhi rather than through Srinagar or Jammu — a move made India's first Buddhist-majority union territory, and one that gave the region a distinct administrative identity for the first time since the Dogra annexation nearly two centuries earlier.

The sites mapped here draw on that long Namgyal and monastic past — the palaces, forts and gompas of a Himalayan Buddhist kingdom that outlasted its own conquest by centuries in its architecture and religious life, even after it lost its political independence.
